"Sir," began Elara, her spirit kindling at the injustice of the charge, "we were merely enjoying the evening air. Henry's diligence is not a matter for us to govern."

She gave Henry a look that was full of unspoken sympathy, a look he answered with a brief, almost imperceptible nod. He too had risen to his feet when his uncle appeared and now stood with a kind of rigid formality, his hands clenched at his sides.

"A word with you, Henry," he said.
He did not move, but stood waiting, compelling his nephew to attend him there in the garden, as if he were a clerk to be reprimanded in a place of public passage. The moon, a silver sliver, had risen above the trees, and its faint, cold light gave to his severe features the immobility of a stone effigy on a tomb.
"I am not a harsh guardian," he began, a statement which he believed to be the simple truth. "I have provided for you, educated you, given you opportunities far beyond what your own father, my unfortunate brother, could ever have offered. Do not forget it."
"I am not permitted to forget it," Henry retorted, a spark of his earlier fire breaking through his restraint.
Mr. Thorne's eyes narrowed. "Do not take that tone with me. I am your guardian, not your fellow-debater. You will return to your room. You will re-read the letters of Cicero, and you will write me a one-page summary of his arguments on the nature of friendship, in Latin. It will be on my desk before you go to bed. The night is long; you will have ample time to complete it if you apply yourself."
Without waiting for a reply, he turned and walked away, his heavy footsteps crunching on the gravel, a relentless, departing rhythm.
Henry stood alone in the moonlit garden. The fragrant air, which moments before had been a balm, now seemed to choke him. He felt a profound humiliation, a rage that was all the more bitter for being impotent. He was a man in years, with a man's thoughts and passions, yet he was treated as a recalcitrant schoolboy. His uncle's words had been designed to strike at the very root of his pride; to remind him of his dependence, to devalue his intellect by framing it as a mere commodity that had been purchased.
He sank back onto the bench, not with the languor of a dreamer, but with the heavy weariness of a prisoner. The beauty of the night was lost to him; the moon was a cold cinder, the scent of the roses a funereal perfume. He saw his life stretching before him, a long, straight road paved with his uncle's intentions, a road he must walk under a perpetual, joyless sense of obligation.
He thought of Agnes's words: "You have a good heart; do not be too proud to show it." How could he show his heart, when it was daily encased in the ice of his uncle's displeasure? He thought of Elara's philosophy of pride, of Mr. Finch standing silent and unmoved before a tirade. Finch could walk away; Finch had a home to go to, a place where he was master. Henry's home was his prison; his master lived with him, slept under the same roof, and held the key not only to the door but to his future.
A light appeared in an upper window of the house; the window of the little room that served as his study. His uncle had no doubt gone to his own library, confident that his orders would be obeyed. The light was a summons, a beacon calling him to his sentence: Cicero and the nature of friendship. A bitter irony. What did this cold, calculating Roman know of the friendship Henry craved, the free and equal communion of spirits he had enjoyed for a brief hour with his cousins? What did his uncle, who demanded duty instead of affection, know of any bond that was not based on power and obligation?
For a long time he did not move. He was lost in a labyrinth of resentment and despair. He felt a wild impulse to disobey; to walk out of the gate and never return. But where would he go? What could he do? He had been trained for nothing but the life of a gentleman scholar, a life that required the very capital he lacked. His pride, the "thought-proud" nature Agnes had so gently named, was the only thing he truly possessed, and it was a pride that his uncle sought to systematically dismantle.
Presently, another light appeared, this one in the window of the drawing-room. He could just make out two figures moving behind the curtains. Elara and Agnes. They had not retired; perhaps they were talking of him, of the scene they had just witnessed. He imagined their conversation: Elara's sharp, indignant defence of him; Agnes's quiet, sorrowful sympathy. The thought was a small comfort, a single warm ember in the cold grate of his misery. It was for Agnes, for the hope of proving worthy of her good opinion, that he found the strength to rise.
With a heavy sigh, he turned his back on the moonlit garden and walked towards the house, towards the lonely light in the upper window. The path that led to the door felt like the last mile of a condemned man's walk. He was going to obey, not out of duty to his uncle, but out of a deeper, more complex allegiance to the affections that made his dependent life bearable. He would write the essay, and he would make it the most elegant, most incisive piece of Latin prose he had ever composed. He would meet his uncle's tyranny not with sullen rebellion, but with a display of the very intellect his uncle sought to both cultivate and control. It was a small, cold victory, but it was the only one available to him. His pride, forced from all other outlets, took refuge in the last redoubt of his mind. He would be clever, because he was not allowed to be anything else.

The man who had been discoursing on the nature of his own soul vanished; in his place sat a silent, stony-faced labourer, his gaze fixed on the grass at his feet, his whole being contracted into an attitude of passive, unyielding resistance. He smiled as he said it, to show it was a jest, but his eyes held a petty gleam of reproof.

"You are, Donne, you are," boomed Mr. Malone, who was staring at Shirley's animated face with an air of bovine admiration. "A very devil to wrestle with, is pride."

"And he tried to wound that man's soul, which ought to be the strongest part of him," Shirley retorted, gesturing towards William. "To be cruel to cruelty is a justice, my dear, not a sin. William Farren slowly raised his head. He looked at Shirley, and the hard, defensive mask was gone. In his eyes was a look of profound, almost painful gratitude, a look that spoke of long-held bitterness momentarily washed away. He did not smile, but his whole rugged countenance seemed to soften.

"Miss Shirley," he said, his voice low and a little hoarse. "You spoke up for me. You, a lady. You shamed him for me." He paused, searching for words, a rare difficulty for him. "My wife, she says there's no good in gentry, that they're all cut from the same cloth as masters. I've often thought it myself. But she's wrong. And so was I." He looked from Shirley's animated face to Caroline's gentle one. "Ye're true ladies, the pair of ye. Ye have good hearts. God bless you for it."

He stood up then, settling the child on his hip. The two little girls, who had been huddled together like frightened sparrows, rose with him. He put on his hat, but it was not the surly gesture of a man asserting his independence; it was the simple action of a man preparing to go home.

"Good-night, Miss Keeldar. Good-night, Miss Caroline," he said. And with his little family trailing him, he walked away through the twilight, his back as straight as it had been when he faced the curates, but with a different kind of pride in its bearing now.

Shirley and Caroline watched him go. The western sky was now a deep, bruised purple, and the star of evening, the star Shirley had seen on the zone of her Titaness, burned with a steady, liquid light.

"He will go home and tell his wife that he was wrong," Shirley said quietly, almost to herself. "And she will not believe him. And they will argue. And tomorrow, he will come to work in the gardens at Fieldhead, and he will work with a kind of fury, to prove to himself, and to me, and to the ghost of Mr. Donne, that a man's labour is his own patent of nobility. The pride that builds, Caroline. We saw it tonight."

"I saw a good man insulted," said Caroline, "and a kind friend defend him. I was frightened, Shirley."

"I was not," said Shirley, and she was her old self again, the visionary and the pragmatist all at once. "I was alive. It is what I told you, Caroline. Stay out of the church, and you will see unusual things. You will see heaven and hell contending in a green churchyard. You will see a man's soul." She took Caroline's arm, her grip firm and warm. "Come, let us not go into the rectory. The air in there will be thick with the smoke of Mr. Donne's singed vanity. Let us walk on the moor. My mother, Nature, has more to say to us yet, and her voice does not whine or preach."

And so they left the place of headstones and arguments, and turned their faces towards the dark, open expanse of the moor, walking together under the vast and silent witness of the stars. The world of men, with its petty hierarchies and its proud, foolish curates, fell away behind them; before them lay the heath, and the wind, and the grand, undegenerate night.

The quiet, the order, the safety of it, which she usually took for granted, enveloped her like a blessing. The Titan had been roused, not the glorious, heaven-born mother of Shirley's vision, but a more ancient, terrible one: the Titan of human conflict, of pride, and of rage. And its heavy tread was shaking the very ground beneath their feet.

The knitting fell from Hortense's hands. Mrs. Pryor gave a little gasp and pressed a hand to her heart. Caroline felt the blood drain from her face, leaving her cold and numb. Only Shirley seemed unmoved.

"And?" she prompted, her voice level. "What is his message?"

The footman swallowed. "He says, miss... he says the men are gathering. On Blackwood Edge. They have masks, and pikes, and some have guns. They mean to march on the Hollow. On Mr. Moore's mill." He paused, and his next words fell into the utter stillness of the room like stones into a deep well.

Caroline thought of Robert's face, as she had last seen it, pale and strained, his eyes full of a weary defiance. She thought of his sister, Hortense, whose rigid pride was even now being paid for with her brother's peril. She thought of her own long, silent love, a feeling she had believed to be a weakness, a source of pain. But now, it felt like a source of strength, a fire to match Shirley's.

"I am ready," she said.

Martin returned, breathless, carrying a polished mahogany box. Shirley opened it and took out two heavy, silver-inlaid duelling pistols. She checked the priming with an expert's touch, handed one to Caroline, and tucked the other into the waistband of her own riding habit.

"Do you know how to use it?" Shirley asked.

"My uncle taught me, once," Caroline murmured, the cold weight of the weapon in her hand a terrifying and steadying reality.

"Point it, and pull the trigger. Pray you do not have to," Shirley said grimly. "Now, up. We have a ten-mile ride, and a man's life at the end of it."

With Martin's help, Caroline was thrown into the saddle of the tall horse. She felt high, unsteady, her heart hammering against her ribs. Beside her, Shirley was already mounted on Zephyr, the black mare stamping and tossing her head, sensing the urgency in the air.

"Which way, Miss Keeldar?" Martin asked. "The road is full of men."

"We are not taking the road. We go up the Nab, and across the heather. God be with you, Martin. Bar the gates behind us."

She wheeled her horse, and without a backward glance, spurred it out of the stable yard and up the steep track that led towards the open moor. Caroline gritted her teeth, clutched the reins and the pistol, and kicked the powerful horse beneath her into a canter, following the dark, flying shape of her friend into the wild, uncertain night. The lights of the village fell away below them, and they were alone with the wind, the dark immensity of the heath, and the blood-red stain that pulsed on the horizon like a dying heart.
